Pins an initialized cache page while excluding truncate invalidation.

 The callback runs while the address-space invalidation read lock is
 held. Pages starting at or beyond EOF are rejected before allocation or
 admission. The callback must validate its exact byte range and publish the read-only
 PTE together with its file-mapping reference before returning. Truncate
 submits mapping invalidation before detaching the cache entry, but that
 submission may be deferred while an MM is busy. The mapping owner must
 retain the pin until PTE removal and TLB invalidation actually complete.
 Callback failure keeps a successfully initialized in-range page resident
 and charged, so another access can reuse it.

Runs `f` with the initialized resident folio at `index`, if present.
 Missing or non-uptodate folios are reported as `None`.

Visits a bounded resident-page snapshot without populating holes.

 Holds one invalidate read guard through the batch, including EOF sampling
 and data copying in `visit`. At most [`pagecache::FolioBatch::CAPACITY`]
 pages are visited after a single index snapshot; absent pages are `None`.
 Retained initialization failures propagate instead of becoming holes.
 Callbacks must not reenter this mapping, change folio state, or wait for
 another folio. Returns the number visited, including a breaking page.

 # Errors

 Propagates index-range overflow, filesystem initialization, or callback
 errors. Earlier callback progress remains committed to its caller.

Prepares and dirties a cached folio for a shared write fault.

Takes responsibility for initializing a locked resident folio.

 The folio may be newly allocated or retained after an earlier failed
 read. Initialize its entire contents on every successful attempt;
 do not rely on contents left by a failed attempt. The same index can
 be submitted again after failure or replacement; each token is a distinct
 initialization responsibility. Release attempt-local resources on every
 completion, including failure, rather than deduplicating by index.

 Returning success means the read was submitted or completed. Complete
 the token only after the entire folio is initialized, including zeroes for
 holes, unwritten extents and the tail beyond EOF. The filesystem owns
 the read boundary and must report incomplete backing reads as errors;
 a later EOF sample must not reinterpret an already completed read.
 `FolioRead::complete` publishes uptodate on success; failure or dropping
 the token leaves it non-uptodate for retry without exposing partial data.
 Submission failure must release the token before returning the error.
 Submission errors propagate unchanged. After accepted submission, a
 failed completion is observed as `VfsError::Io`: the folio records
 initialization success, not a second copy of the backing I/O result.

 Runs with the folio locked and the cache index lock released. Do not

 completion must not require the mapping index, inode data or invalidate
 locks: their holders can wait for this folio. It must own every backing
 resource it needs after this callback returns.

The table's native chunk-copy primitive, mirroring Linux
 `f_op->copy_file_range`: copies up to `len` bytes from `input` at
 `input_pos` into this table's file at `output_pos` and returns the
 bytes actually copied. `None` means the table carries no native
 implementation — the generic buffered pump serves the pair, and only
 same-superblock pairs at that. An implementation judges input
 compatibility itself and reports `EXDEV` for inputs it cannot serve,
 so the VFS performs no identity comparison anywhere. The VFS also
 issues one empty-range (`len == 0`) query as pair admission, at the
 point where Linux compares the two `f_op->copy_file_range` slots.
 That query is the pair's verdict, so an implementation must answer it
 without side effects and with the answer a data-carrying call would
 give: `None` exactly when the table carries no primitive, and the
 input judgement ahead of any empty-range short-circuit.

Polls an open file description.

 `None` mirrors Linux `file->f_op->poll == NULL`: the file type provides
 no poll handler. [`VfsFile::poll`] then falls back to reporting the file
 as always ready (`DEFAULT_POLLMASK`, Linux `vfs_poll`), while `epoll_ctl`
 refuses to register such a target with `EPERM` (Linux `file_can_poll`,
 `fs/eventpoll.c`) — which is how a user-space runtime learns that a
 descriptor has to stay in blocking mode (the Go runtime's poller relies
 on exactly that for regular files).

 Providing this method *is* the capability: regular files and directories
 do not, so no implementation needs to declare pollability separately.

 The handler must be side-effect free apart from polling readiness; both
 wait paths (`poll`/`select` and `epoll`) call it to observe readiness.

Runs the full Linux check table in order and returns the effective copy
 length: directories are rejected with `EISDIR`, every non-regular fd
 (pipes, sockets, devices) with `EINVAL`, a destination opened `O_APPEND`
 with `EBADF` (the copy would land at the wrong offset), and a pair the
 destination cannot serve with `EXDEV`. The range checks then run in
 Linux's order: an unsigned wrap of the request is reported as
 `EOVERFLOW`, the request is shortened to the source EOF, and the
 destination's own ceiling applies — a start at or past the maximum file
 size is `EFBIG` and the count is clamped to what the destination can
 hold. Overlapping ranges within one inode are rejected with `EINVAL` so
 the chunked copy can never read bytes it has already rewritten; a
 zero-length request never overlaps and remains a no-op.

 into explicit starts under the position locks, `verify_copy_file_range`

 an unservable pair reports `EXDEV` even when the request is empty — and
 the pump copies between the local positions. Resolution, checks, copy and
 the position commit share one critical section (Linux `fdget_pos`), so
 concurrent transfers on a shared open file description neither duplicate
 ranges nor clobber a concurrent seek. [`TransferPosition::At`] sides run at the given offsets and are
 advanced by the transferred count; `f_pos` is untouched for them. Like
 Linux `vfs_copy_file_range`, the copy allows partial success: an error

 published positions always describe the bytes the destination actually

Performs an initialization routine once and only once. The given closure
 will be executed if this is the first time `call_once` has been called,
 and otherwise the routine will *not* be invoked.

 This method will spin-wait if another thread is currently performing
 initialization.

 When this function returns, it is guaranteed that some initialization
 has run and completed (it may not be the closure specified). The
 returned pointer will point to the result from the closure that was
 run.

 # Panics

 This function will panic if the [`Once`] previously panicked while attempting
 to initialize. This is similar to the poisoning behaviour of `std::sync`'s
 primitives.

 # Examples

 ```
 use klazy;

 static INIT: klazy::Once<usize> = klazy::Once::new();

 fn get_cached_val() -> usize {
     *INIT.call_once(expensive_computation)
 }

 fn expensive_computation() -> usize {
     // ...
 # 2
 }
 ```

Marks a function as a unit test.

 # Example

 ```rust
 use unittest::def_test;

 #[def_test]
 fn test_addition() {
     let a = 2 + 2;
     assert_eq!(a, 4);
 }
 ```

 The test function can optionally return `TestResult`. If it doesn't return anything,
 the function body is wrapped to return `TestResult::Ok` on success.

 # Attributes
 - `#[def_test]` - Normal test
 - `#[def_test(ignore)]` - Test will be skipped
 - `#[def_test(should_panic)]` - Test expects panic (not fully supported in no_std)
 - `#[def_test(user)]` - Test runs in a newly constructed user task
 - `#[def_test(serial)]` - Test must run sequentially (not parallel-safe)
